leads.title: Bombing attack on convoy - Charles Gardner, 14 July 1940 (RAF Museum object X003-1795)
leads.licence_evidence: The page gives no copyright or licence statement. The maker is the BBC. A secondary page (spitfiresite.com) mentions 'Crown Copyright' but does not clearly tie it to the audio. Copyright in a 1940 UK recording may have expired, but nothing on the page says so.
leads.what: BBC actuality recording made at a real event: Charles Gardner's live commentary as Junkers Ju 87 dive-bombers attack a Channel convoy ('Bread') off Dover on 14 July 1940. The page says Spitfires intercept, anti-aircraft fire can be heard, a Ju 87 crashes, and a dogfight with Bf 109s follows. Spitfiresite says the crew recorded from a house overlooking the port and then from a nearby cliff, and that the report is about 8 minutes long and was sent uncut. The RAF Museum page gives no duration, and no audio player loaded.
leads.fit: This is the only real recording of actual Ju 87 formations attacking that I found. Jumo 211 engines from a real Stuka raid would be in the background, so it fits the Ju 87 formation subject better than any substitute engine.
leads.concerns: (1) Gardner talks over almost the whole recording, so clean drone sections are probably short or missing. (2) The aircraft are distant and mixed with AA fire, bombs and RAF fighters. (3) It is a BBC recording. It is news actuality, not the BBC Sound Effects library, but check that it fits your rules. (4) The licence is unknown and no download is offered. (5) The RAF Museum and spitfiresite.com give different dates (14 July vs 13 June).

leads.title: Spitfires and Bf-109 Flyby by Fight2FlyPhoto (Freesound 142902)
leads.licence_evidence: The search snippet shows only the title and uploader, not the licence. It comes from the same uploader as the two Fight2FlyPhoto Bf 109 leads already found (142898, 242179), so it may carry the same licence. Check before use.
leads.what: The search title says it is a flyby of Spitfires and a Bf 109. The uploader's other Bf 109 items name a Daimler-Benz engine ('Bf-109 - Daimler-Benz Run-Up'), and a Cities and Memory re-post of 242179 describes their 109 as a restored Bf 109E-3 with a DB 601. That suggests this is a DB 601 inverted V12 in flight, but the snippet does not confirm it. Date, place, mic setup and length are not visible.
leads.fit: An inverted-V12 German engine in flight. The DB 601 is close in size and layout to the Jumo 211 (both about 34-35 L inverted V12s). It is the airborne counterpart to the ground runs already found.
leads.concerns: (1) Merlin-engined Spitfires are mixed in, so a clean 109-only section may be short. (2) It is a flyby rather than a steady drone, and it is one aircraft, not a formation. (3) The licence is not verified from here.

leads.title: Fw 190 D 13 start up and moreYT (YouTube uf7nyTdwsHU)
leads.licence_evidence: I could not read the page (rate-limited twice). The snippet shows no licence. Most YouTube videos use the Standard YouTube License, so this is usable only if the page shows 'Creative Commons Attribution'.
leads.what: The search title says it is a start-up and more of an Fw 190 D-13. Forum threads say the only original D-13 (ex-Champlin, now Flying Heritage & Combat Armor Museum, 'Yellow 10') has made engine runs with its Jumo 213. The snippet gives no uploader, date, place, length or mic details.
leads.fit: The Jumo 213 is the Jumo 211's direct successor (Junkers inverted V12), so it is the closest engine family to the Ju 87 that still runs.
leads.concerns: (1) The licence is probably not free. (2) It is a ground run or start-up, not a formation in flight. (3) The title ends in 'YT', so it may be edited, and it may carry music or narration. I could not check either. (4) If it is free, the audio would have to be taken from the video.

leads.title: Messerschmitt Bf 109 G14 Lowpasses and original Daimler DB605 Engine Sound (YouTube eqAz2GSmqW0)
leads.licence_evidence: Two fetch attempts were rate-limited. The snippet shows no licence. Usable only if the page shows a Creative Commons Attribution licence.
leads.what: The search title says it shows low passes of a Bf 109 G-14 with an original DB 605 engine, apparently filmed at an airshow. The snippet gives no recordist, place, date or length. Related snippets say the only DB 605-powered 109s flying are in Germany (Messerschmitt-Stiftung, Hangar 10 / Zirchow).
leads.fit: A real DB 605 inverted V12 in flight, which is what the brief asks for as a Jumo 211 substitute.
leads.concerns: (1) The licence is probably standard YouTube (not usable). (2) It is a single aircraft making passes, not a sustained formation drone. (3) There may be crowd or PA noise, or music, which I could not check.

leads.title: "Raid on Berlin": actuality recording of an RAF bombing raid over Berlin, 4 September 1943 (AWM S00199)
leads.licence_evidence: The AWM page states that copyright has expired and the item is in the public domain, marked with the Public Domain Mark 1.0. The standard copying note also says personal and non-commercial use is permitted, which suits this project.
leads.what: A real wartime recording made aboard Lancaster 'F for Freddy' of 207 Squadron RAF during a raid on Berlin on 4 September 1943. Wynford Vaughan Thomas (BBC) narrates and Reginald Pidsley was the sound recordist. It covers the approach, searchlights and bomb release, and an attack by a German night fighter that the crew shoots down. It is 6 min 32 s long, on a 12-inch 78 rpm mono disc.
leads.fit: Weak fallback only. It is a verified public-domain WW2 recording made inside a bomber, with a continuous multi-engine drone.
leads.concerns: (1) The engines are Merlins (upright V12), not Jumo, heard from inside the aircraft. (2) There is narration and crew intercom over most of it. (3) The AWM also lists permission requirements for commercial use, which does not matter for a non-commercial game. (4) It is not a Ju 87 sound.

leads.title: File:Bf109g10.ogv (Wikimedia Commons video)
leads.licence_evidence: Only the title and URL appeared in search results. The description, author and licence were not visible, and Commons is blocked from here.
leads.what: A Commons video file named for a Bf 109 G-10. The search showed it in 'Category:Messerschmitt Bf 109 warbirds', which suggests a modern warbird rather than wartime film, but that is not certain. Source, date, length and whether it has sound are unknown.
leads.fit: If it is a modern recording with sound of a DB 605 Bf 109 G-10, it would be a useful inverted-V12 in-flight reference.
leads.concerns: (1) Everything about it is unverified. (2) It may be wartime film (excluded) or silent. (3) A Commons licence may be CC BY-SA, which does not qualify. (4) The low resolution (a 512x288 category appeared nearby) suggests an old upload.

found.gaps:
I still found no free, real recording of a Jumo 211, Jumo 213 or Ju 87 formation. The leads above are weak: the strongest real Ju 87 recording (Gardner, 1940) has an unknown licence and commentary over it, the DB 601/605 and Jumo 213 leads were seen only as snippets with unknown licences, and the only verified public-domain item is a Merlin bomber interior.

What I checked and ruled out:
- **University of Alabama in Huntsville archive** (https://archives.uah.edu/repositories/2/archival_objects/93529). It holds a wartime Fw 190 recording (start-up, taxi, take-off, dive, low-level attack), but its catalogue references are 'BBC Sound Effects EC 500C'. It is a BBC SFX library item with no licence and no digital copy, so it is excluded. Related items 20220025-20220038 are 'all BBC Sounds'.
- **IL-2 forum Ju 88 clip** (https://forum.il2sturmovik.com/topic/10021-stuka-purring-is-absolutely-not-jumo-211/). A post by BOBC (2014) attaches 'Ju88AJumo211_Genuine_extract.wav', described as a real Jumo 211 Ju 88A start-up, idle and taxi. Its source and licence are not stated, and it is probably from the wartime BBC captured-aircraft recordings, so I did not list it.
- **ATAG forum thread** 'Actual Jumo 211 and DB601 engine sounds offer of help' (theairtacticalassaultgroup.com t=12636). Robots-blocked, so unread.
- **Commercial libraries (excluded).** Pole Position Production / Sonniss 'Messerschmitt Bf109 G4' (Max Lachmann).
- **Cities and Memory.** The Audioboom/Mixcloud 'Messerschmidt BF-109 startup' is a re-post of Fight2FlyPhoto 242179 (already found).
- **NMUSAF 'ISR Tour' audio on DVIDS** (Bf 109G-10, Fw 190D-9). Narration only; the transcript has no engine sounds.
- **Fight2FlyPhoto Fw-190 items** (143562, 161104, 161107). The FHC Fw 190 A-5 has a BMW 801 radial, so these do not fit a Stuka.
- **AWM CC BY-NC field recordings.** The AWM has CC BY-NC 3.0 AU field recordings from 2014 (e.g. Spitfire S05933 at https://www.awm.gov.au/collection/C2093388, Meteor S05926), but no German aircraft.

Restorations and running engines:
- No Jumo 211 has run publicly yet. FHCAM's Ju 87R-2 moved to The Roost (Bentonville, AR) in June 2025. Mike Nixon / Vintage V-12s overhauled its Jumo 211, and Vintage Aviation News says it will likely be the first operational Jumo 211 to fly in over 50 years.
- The American Heritage Museum's Ju 87D-5 is being restored in the Czech Republic.
- When either engine first runs, the owners' own footage is unlikely to be CC-licensed, but a US government (DVIDS) crew at a later airshow might film it. Worth re-checking in 2027.
- No Flug Werk or other Fw 190 D-9 with a Jumo 213 was confirmed flying. The 2010-era projects (Yagen/MAM, White 1 Foundation, Vormezeele) had no flight reports in what I read.

Not tried or blocked:
- YouTube pages were rate-limited, so licences for YouTube leads (including Fw 190 D-13 start-ups, Hangar 10 'Schwarze 8' G-6 and Messerschmitt-Stiftung G-4 'Red 7') are unchecked. Most are probably standard YouTube licence.
- I did not use Freesound-metadata mirrors (Hugging Face datasets, Openverse) or Wikipedia/OSMand copies of Commons pages, because of the no-mirror rule.
- Wikidata and en.wikipedia File pages would not load.
- IWM pages would not load, and IWM uses its own non-commercial licence, not CC.
- NARA's captured German sound recordings (RG 242) are mostly speeches, with almost none online.

Suggestions for a later pass:
- Read the licences of Freesound 142902 and of the two YouTube leads directly.
- Ask the RAF Museum or AWM whether they hold a copy of the Gardner 1940 recording, or other BBC/ABC 1940-41 actuality of Stuka raids (Tobruk, Greece, Crete, Malta), marked public domain like AWM S00199.

verdicts.rule_broken: Licence must be CC0/PD/CC BY/CC BY-NC: the page has no rights or licence statement, and it offers no audio to download.
verdicts.reason: I read the page. The URL is real and matches the claim: 'Bombing attack on convoy - Charles Gardner, 14 July 1940', object X003-1795, maker British Broadcasting Corporation, production date 14 July 1940. The description names Ju 87s bombing a convoy, Spitfire interception, audible AA fire, a Ju 87 crash and a Bf 109 dogfight. It is BBC news actuality, not the BBC Sound Effects library, so that rule is not broken. But the page has no copyright or licence text, no player, no download and no duration, so as listed it cannot be used. Gardner also gives running commentary, so clean engine passages are likely short. It is the only lead here with real Ju 87s in it, so it is worth finding a copy of the same recording that carries an explicit public-domain or copyright-expired statement (see 'missed'). The 14 July date on the page matches the well-known date of this broadcast. The 13 June date on spitfiresite looks like that site's error.

So I verified 4 of 6 leads by reading their pages, but could not check the Freesound 142902 and Commons Bf109g10.ogv snippets. Sources not tried that should be: (1) A public-domain copy of the same Charles Gardner 14 July 1940 Ju 87 convoy recording. The AWM holds many BBC actuality 78s marked 'copyright expired - public domain' (as with S00199), and the IWM sound archive also holds it. This is the only real Ju 87 formation audio found, so a PD-marked copy is the top priority. (2) A YouTube search with the Creative Commons filter for 'Jumo 213', 'Fw 190 D-9 engine run', 'Ta 152', 'Jumo 211 engine run', 'DB 605 engine run' and 'Messerschmitt-Stiftung Bf 109 G-6/G-4' (D-FWME, Hangar 10). (3) Freesound tag searches such as jumo, daimler-benz, db605, db601, bf109 and fw190 (blocked here, so a manual check). (4) Commons categories 'Junkers Jumo 211', 'Junkers Jumo 213' and 'Messerschmitt Bf 109 warbirds' (blocked, manual check). (5) The Avia S-199, the post-war Czech Bf 109 G airframe fitted with a real Jumo 211F, and the Jumo 211-engined early CASA 2.111: look for any museum engine run at the Kbely (Prague) museum, the Israeli Air Force Museum or the Spanish Museo del Aire. (6) Any Ju 87 restoration engine run (Flying Heritage & Combat Armor Museum has been reported to own a Ju 87 under restoration) and FHCAM's own Fly Day media for its Bf 109 E (DB 601) and Fw 190 D-13. (7) Vintage V-12s (Tehachapi) test-stand runs of DB 605 or Jumo engines. Check every one of these for an explicit CC BY, CC BY-NC, CC0 or PD licence before use.

leads.title: HMAS Adelaide, Adelaide class guided missile Frigate - operational sounds (S04691)
leads.licence_evidence: The page says: 'Item copyright: © Australian War Memorial'. It is licensed under CC BY-NC 3.0 Australia. Copying provisions: 'Only personal, non-commercial, research and study use permitted.'
leads.what: A Defence Public Relations (DPR) sound-effect tape recorded aboard the frigate HMAS Adelaide on 29 June 1984. The maker is Ron Townsend. It is on DAT, 48 kHz/16-bit stereo, 1 hr 4 min. The contents are split into exterior and interior segments. They include 'chaff launcher loading and firing', missile loading, the 76 mm gun, the Harpoon launcher, Phalanx firing, engine room, wake, and a replenishment at sea with USS Taluga. No place is given. The page does not state mic placement, but other tapes in the same DPR series are described as 'close perspective'.
leads.fit: This is the closest naval match I found in the AWM catalogue. It is a tube launcher on a warship's deck firing a round from close by, recorded at a real event by a service recordist. The same series also holds the 'Mortar - operational sounds' tape that the first search found. It is useful if a shipboard, deck-level launch thump is wanted rather than a land mortar.
leads.concerns: A chaff launcher is not a depth-charge projector. Some chaff rounds are rocket-boosted, so there may be a whoosh after the launch thump, and the page does not say which round was fired. The chaff takes are inside a 64-minute tape, and the page gives no track timings. The recording is from the 1980s, not WW2. CC BY-NC is fine only while the game stays non-commercial.

leads.title: CGC Kimball tests SRBOC system during final sea trials
leads.licence: public domain (US government work), not checked on the page
leads.licence_evidence: DVIDS b-roll filmed by US Coast Guard personnel is a US federal government work. I did not read the page itself, so I could not check for a copyright note or a credit to a civilian photographer.
leads.what: From the title: the US Coast Guard cutter Kimball test-firing its Mk 36 SRBOC launcher during final sea trials. The search results also show related DVIDS images of Kimball's final sea trials off the Hawaiian Islands, including Phalanx test firings. Length, mic and camera position are unknown.
leads.fit: SRBOC is a fixed mortar-type tube launcher on a ship's deck. A camera-mic recording of a test firing could give a real shipboard 'tube thump' close by, which is near what a K-gun or Y-gun firing would sound like.
leads.concerns: I did not read the page, so I don't know whether the audio is the original sync sound or has music added, how close the camera was, or the length. Many SRBOC rounds are rocket-boosted, which adds a whoosh. A DoD mirror of the video exists, but I did not try it, as instructed.

That is my inference and is not confirmed.

leads.fit: This is a weak fit. A K-gun or Y-gun threw its charge with a black-powder impulse cartridge, so a black-powder discharge has the right character. A cannon is sharper and more of a boom than a mortar thump. Use it only as a fallback or a layer.

found.gaps:
I found no real recording of an actual depth-charge thrower, Hedgehog, Squid or Limbo firing under an acceptable licence. All the leads above are proxies: shipboard chaff-launcher tubes, land mortars and a black-powder cannon.

What I checked at the AWM:
- No search turned up a Limbo, Ikara or depth-charge sound recording for the River-class destroyer escorts (Yarra, Parramatta, Stuart, Derwent, Swan, Torrens).
- I read the DPR/Ron Townsend 'operational sounds' tapes for HMAS Adelaide (S04691), HMAS Canberra (S04693, https://www.awm.gov.au/collection/C1240477) and HMAS Launceston (S04701, https://www.awm.gov.au/collection/C1240485). I also read HMAS Brisbane 2001 (S04237, https://www.awm.gov.au/collection/C1169841) and the Brisbane 1971 Vietnam gunline actuality recording (S02857, https://awm.gov.au/collection/C1002469).
- None of them lists Limbo, Ikara, depth charges or torpedo tubes. The Canberra and Brisbane tapes have only 5-inch and 76 mm guns and missiles.
- The AWM advanced-search page is blocked to automated access (robots), so I could not browse the full Sound facet. An in-person or browser search of the AWM catalogue for 'Limbo' with the Sound facet is still worth doing.
- AWM RAN film items such as 'Fleet Bombardment' F11197 (https://www.awm.gov.au/collection/C1171238) are silent, and the 'Navy in Focus' items are film newsreels, which the rules exclude.

Possible but doubtful: AWM S03297, 'Operational sounds of United States military aircraft, armour and weapons used during the war in Vietnam' (https://www.awm.gov.au/collection/C1079277, CC BY-NC, page read). Track 16 is a 'close up of mortar firing'. But the recordist is 'unknown', the source credit is only 'AWM Research Grants Scheme', and the track list includes an out-of-context 'crowd cheering' track. It may be a compilation drawn from an effects library, so I left it out of the leads.

Other notes:
- Duke Sonic Dictionary has 'Cannon Shots' (https://sonicdictionary.duke.edu/items/cannon-shots.html, CC BY-NC 4.0, page read): an iPhone 5 recording of real cannons at Williamsburg, with a spoken 'fire!'. It is a weaker version of the NPS cannon lead.
- The USS Sealion 1944 submarine attack recording (https://ussnautilus.org/sealions-sounds/) is real WW2 audio but not a thrower, and no licence is stated.
- HNSA's historic naval sound page could not be fetched.
- WW2 and 1950s films of Hedgehog, Limbo and K-guns (IWM film, CriticalPast, NFB stock shots, Smithsonian) are films or newsreels, or under commercial licences, so I excluded them.
- I found no US Navy public-domain video of a Mk 9, Hedgehog or Mousetrap firing. These weapons left US service long ago, and DVIDS has only stills of museum K-guns and Y-guns.
- Next steps: someone with access should open the DVIDS and Freesound leads to confirm the sync sound and licence. They could also look for DVIDS video of Mk 32 torpedo-tube 'air slug' firings. Only stills turned up in search, but a video would give a close compressed-air ASW launch thump. Freesound CC0 recordings of fireworks mortar-tube launches (a black-powder lift charge in a tube, mechanically close to a K-gun) are another option, but the search snippets did not show titles or licences.

leads.title: NASA Crash Tests eVTOL Concept (Lift+Cruise full-scale drop test, Nov 2022), with highlight video
leads.licence_evidence: Made by NASA's own staff: the page credits the video to Gary Banziger, and the images.nasa.gov metadata names Gary Banziger as photographer (owner gbanzige, center LRC). The page has no reuse statement of its own and links only to NASA Brand & Usage Guidelines. The metadata has no copyright field.
leads.what: A full-scale 'Lift+Cruise' eVTOL test body, with an overhead mass standing in for the wing, rotors and battery, was hoisted at NASA Langley's LandIR gantry. Pyrotechnic cutters released it and it swung down into the ground with crash dummies aboard. The page says 'the overhead structure collapsed' and the vehicle 'was destroyed beyond expectations'. Video is credited to Gary Banziger, filmed around 9 Nov 2022 (date taken from the filename). The direct MP4 on the page is https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/larc-110922-liftandcruisedroptest-highlights-banziger-1.mp4. images.nasa.gov has a 2:27 version, 1920x1080, with a 2-channel 44.1 kHz audio track: http://images-assets.nasa.gov/video/2022-H1_V_Lift&CruiseDropTest-5/2022-H1_V_Lift&CruiseDropTest-5~orig.mp4 (219 MiB). Mic placement is not stated.
leads.fit: The best structural failure found. A real airframe crushes and its overhead structure collapses on impact, and there is a downloadable original from NASA with an audio track. The sound should be crunching, buckling structure rather than an explosion.
leads.concerns: It is called a 'highlights' reel, so it may carry music, narration or edits over the field sound; the audio content is not stated anywhere. The airframe is a modern composite test article, not an aluminium warbird. The impact speed and surface are not stated. I could not read the .srt captions to check for narration.
